recipe.history:
The pineapple — Ananas comosus — arrived in European consciousness in 1493 when Christopher Columbus encountered it on the Caribbean island of Guadeloupe and brought specimens back to Spain, where the royal court received the fruit with a mixture of wonder and incomprehension. The plant itself is native to the area between southern Brazil and Paraguay, where the Tupi-Guaraní people had cultivated it for centuries as both food and symbol. By the 17th century, pineapple cultivation had spread through European colonial networks to Africa, Asia, and the Pacific, and the fruit had become one of the great luxury items of the Western world — a single imported pineapple in 18th-century England could rent for the evening as a dinner party centerpiece before being returned to the greengrocer. In Hawaii, where the fruit was introduced in the early 19th century and industrialized by James Dole in the early 20th, pineapple canning transformed the island economy and gave Americans access to the sweet, acidic fruit year-round. The Dole cannery at its peak was the largest in the world, and the image of pineapple as a Hawaiian product — though the plant is South American — became firmly fixed in the American imagination.

Pineapple on a burger is perhaps the most polarizing topping in the history of the form, and its story is inextricable from the Hawaiian pizza debate that preceded it. The Loco Moco, Hawaii's iconic plate lunch, proved that pineapple and beef could coexist in the same meal, and the teriyaki burger with grilled pineapple — a staple of Hawaiian fast food chains since the 1970s — brought the combination to a mass audience. On the mainland, the "Hawaiian burger" with pineapple, teriyaki glaze, and Swiss cheese became a fixture of casual dining menus in the 1990s. The chemistry is sound: pineapple contains bromelain, a proteolytic enzyme that breaks down muscle fibers and tenderizes meat, and its sugar content caramelizes beautifully on a hot grill. The sweetness and acid provide exactly the contrast that a rich fatty patty needs.

I was firmly in the anti-pineapple-on-burger camp until a summer afternoon at a backyard cookout in Oahu when someone handed me a grilled pineapple ring — slightly charred at the edges, caramelized into something that barely resembled the canned fruit I had dismissed — set atop a beef patty on a toasted bun. The heat had driven off the cloyingness and concentrated the acidity into something almost savory. The pineapple salsa alongside it was a revelation: raw pineapple diced small with jalapeño, red onion, cilantro, and lime had the same role as tomato salsa but with an entirely different register of flavor. I came back from that trip a convert, and I have been grilling pineapple rings for burgers every summer since.

Medium rare is the temperature of conviction — it is what you cook a burger to when you respect the animal, the butcher, and your own palate. The argument against it rests on a misunderstanding of food safety that applies to improperly handled commercial meat, not to freshly ground whole-muscle beef from a trusted source. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the fat within the patty has warmed just enough to flow between the muscle fibers, every bite carries moisture, and the flavor of the beef itself — not just the Maillard crust — comes through fully. With a pineapple ring on top, the sweetness of the fruit and the savory depth of a properly cooked medium rare patty create a harmony that is genuinely surprising, a combination that only works when neither element is overcooked into submission.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
½ jalapeño, seeded and finely minced
1 tsp cornstarch dissolved in 1 tbsp cold water
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — Whisk together flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.
2. Add warm milk, warm water, egg, and softened butter. Mix with the dough hook on low to combine, then medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
4. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a parchment-lined sheet pan, flatten slightly. Cover and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

6. MAKE THE PINEAPPLE SALSA — Combine diced pineapple, jalapeño, red onion, cilantro, and lime juice in a bowl. Season with salt. Let sit at room temperature at least 20 minutes before serving so flavors meld.
7. MAKE THE TERIYAKI GLAZE — Combine soy sauce, brown sugar, mirin, sesame oil, ginger, and garlic in a small saucepan over medium heat.
8. Bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Add cornstarch slurry and whisk until the glaze thickens to coat a spoon, about 2 minutes. Remove from heat.
9. GRILL THE PINEAPPLE — Slice the pineapple into rings about ½-inch thick. Pat dry with paper towels.
10. Toss pineapple rings with neutral oil, brown sugar, and a pinch of salt.
11. Heat a grill pan or cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Grill pineapple rings 2–3 minutes per side until caramelized with char marks. Set aside.

12. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Form into patties ¾-inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
13. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
14. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once.
15. Lay a slice of Swiss cheese on each patty. Cook 2–2½ more minutes.
16. In the last 30 seconds, brush the patties with the teriyaki glaze.
17. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
18. Remove and rest under foil for 3 minutes.
19. TOAST THE BUNS — Split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat, 60–90 seconds.
20. ASSEMBLE — Spread a small amount of remaining teriyaki glaze on the bottom bun.
21. Place a butter lettuce leaf on the bottom bun.
22. Add the Swiss-cheddar-topped patty.
23. Place a grilled pineapple ring on top of the cheese.
24. Spoon pineapple salsa over the pineapple ring.
25. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
